choices.text: Every acid fully releases its hydrogen ions in water, so every acid is equally strong
Acids cannot be weak; they can only be dilute or concentrated
Some acids are weak: they only partly release their hydrogen ions, like the acid in vinegar
Vinegar is not an acid because it is safe to eat

questions.explanation: The trap claim is: All acids are strong acids. In fact Weak acids only partly release their hydrogen ions: vinegar is still acidic, just not strong. Strength describes how fully the acid releases its hydrogen ions, so a weak acid is still a real acid.
questions.prompt: Which statement about acids is correct?

choices.text: The pH 5 solution is more acidic
The pH 3 solution is more acidic, and it is one hundred times more acidic than the pH 5 solution
The two solutions have the same acidity

questions.explanation: Each step on the pH scale is ten times stronger. From pH 5 to pH 3 is two steps towards the acid end, so the acidity rises by ten times ten: one hundred times.
questions.prompt: One solution has pH 3 and another has pH 5. Which statement is correct?

questions.answer: The alkali releases OH- ions, which pair up with the H+ ions from the acid to form water. As the excess H+ ions are used up, the solution moves towards equal ion counts, so the pH rises towards 7, the neutral point.
questions.explanation: Neutralisation is an ion pairing: H+ plus OH- makes water. The pH moves because the ion in excess is being removed, not because the acid is being diluted away.
questions.prompt: Explain, in terms of ions, why adding an alkali to an acid brings the pH towards 7.

questions.answer: The salt is sodium sulfate, because sulfuric acid gives a sulfate. Word equation: sulfuric acid + sodium hydroxide -> sodium sulfate + water.
questions.explanation: A salt takes its second name from the acid: hydrochloric gives a chloride, nitric a nitrate, sulfuric a sulfate. The metal part of the name comes from the alkali, here sodium.
questions.prompt: Sulfuric acid is neutralised by sodium hydroxide. Name the salt formed and write the word equation for the reaction.

choices.text: The equivalence point: the acid has just been exactly neutralised, so an indicator must change colour on the jump
The base has turned into an acid

questions.explanation: Near the equivalence point there is almost no excess ion left, so one drop of base swings the ion balance completely and the pH leaps. An indicator is only useful if its colour change lands on that jump.
questions.prompt: During a titration the pH stays low as base is added, then jumps from 4 to 10 with a single drop. What does the jump show?
